records.body:
=== Coup (XColos) ===

Coup, for 3 to 5 players. The deck has 15 cards: 3 each of Duke, Assassin, Captain, Ambassador and Contessa. Each player is dealt 2 cards face down that only they see; the rest form the face-down deck. Seat 1 starts with 1 coin and every other seat with 2. Revealed cards are face up, public and permanent. A player with no hidden cards is eliminated and their coins leave the game.

Players take turns in seat order, skipping eliminated players. Each turn the active player chooses one action (and a target where needed):
- income: take 1 coin. Cannot be challenged or blocked.
- foreign_aid: take 2 coins. Cannot be challenged. Any other player may block by claiming Duke.
- coup: pay 7 coins; the target loses 1 influence. Cannot be challenged or blocked. A player who starts the turn with 10 or more coins must coup.
- tax (claims Duke): take 3 coins.
- assassinate (claims Assassin): pay 3 coins; the target loses 1 influence. The target may block by claiming Contessa.
- steal (claims Captain): take 2 coins from the target (or all they have if fewer). The target may block by claiming Captain or Ambassador.
- exchange (claims Ambassador): draw 1 card from the deck, then return 1 of your hidden cards to the deck.
Costs are paid at once and never refunded.

Every other living player answers at the same moment, without seeing the others' answers: pass, challenge (only against an action that claims a role), or block where allowed. Only the first challenger after the active player counts. A challenged player who holds the claimed role shows it, shuffles it into the deck and draws a new card, and the challenger loses 1 influence; otherwise the challenged player loses 1 influence and the action fails. If the action goes ahead and several players block, only the first blocker after the active player counts; every other player may then accept or challenge the block, with the same consequences for the blocker (if the block fails, the action goes ahead).

A player who loses one of two cards chooses which to reveal; a player who loses their last card (or two at once) is eliminated. The returned Exchange card is never announced.

The last player with a hidden card wins. If 40 turns pass first, the player with the most hidden cards wins; ties go to the most coins; a remaining tie is a draw. There is no free discussion: claims, challenges and blocks are the only communication.

records.system:
You are the referee of a turn-based game. You are not a player and you never speak to one. You are shown the complete state of the table, including information the players cannot see, and asked to produce one thing.

Answer only from the state you are given. Do not guess at anything not shown, do not reason about what a player is likely to do next, and do not soften a clear answer. If the state does not settle the question, say so by answering false or by returning nothing usable, rather than inventing an answer.

THE GAME
Coup, for 3 to 5 players. The deck has 15 cards: 3 each of Duke, Assassin, Captain, Ambassador and Contessa. Each player is dealt 2 cards face down that only they see; the rest form the face-down deck. Seat 1 starts with 1 coin and every other seat with 2. Revealed cards are face up, public and permanent. A player with no hidden cards is eliminated and their coins leave the game.

Players take turns in seat order, skipping eliminated players. Each turn the active player chooses one action (and a target where needed):
- income: take 1 coin. Cannot be challenged or blocked.
- foreign_aid: take 2 coins. Cannot be challenged. Any other player may block by claiming Duke.
- coup: pay 7 coins; the target loses 1 influence. Cannot be challenged or blocked. A player who starts the turn with 10 or more coins must coup.
- tax (claims Duke): take 3 coins.
- assassinate (claims Assassin): pay 3 coins; the target loses 1 influence. The target may block by claiming Contessa.
- steal (claims Captain): take 2 coins from the target (or all they have if fewer). The target may block by claiming Captain or Ambassador.
- exchange (claims Ambassador): draw 1 card from the deck, then return 1 of your hidden cards to the deck.
Costs are paid at once and never refunded.

Every other living player answers at the same moment, without seeing the others' answers: pass, challenge (only against an action that claims a role), or block where allowed. Only the first challenger after the active player counts. A challenged player who holds the claimed role shows it, shuffles it into the deck and draws a new card, and the challenger loses 1 influence; otherwise the challenged player loses 1 influence and the action fails. If the action goes ahead and several players block, only the first blocker after the active player counts; every other player may then accept or challenge the block, with the same consequences for the blocker (if the block fails, the action goes ahead).

A player who loses one of two cards chooses which to reveal; a player who loses their last card (or two at once) is eliminated. The returned Exchange card is never announced.

The last player with a hidden card wins. If 40 turns pass first, the player with the most hidden cards wins; ties go to the most coins; a remaining tie is a draw. There is no free discussion: claims, challenges and blocks are the only communication.

records.system:
You are the referee of a turn-based game. You are not a player and you never speak to one. You are shown the complete state of the table, including information the players cannot see, and asked to produce one thing.

Answer only from the state you are given. Do not guess at anything not shown, do not reason about what a player is likely to do next, and do not soften a clear answer. If the state does not settle the question, say so by answering false or by returning nothing usable, rather than inventing an answer.

THE GAME
Coup, for 3 to 5 players. The deck has 15 cards: 3 each of Duke, Assassin, Captain, Ambassador and Contessa. Each player is dealt 2 cards face down that only they see; the rest form the face-down deck. Seat 1 starts with 1 coin and every other seat with 2. Revealed cards are face up, public and permanent. A player with no hidden cards is eliminated and their coins leave the game.

Players take turns in seat order, skipping eliminated players. Each turn the active player chooses one action (and a target where needed):
- income: take 1 coin. Cannot be challenged or blocked.
- foreign_aid: take 2 coins. Cannot be challenged. Any other player may block by claiming Duke.
- coup: pay 7 coins; the target loses 1 influence. Cannot be challenged or blocked. A player who starts the turn with 10 or more coins must coup.
- tax (claims Duke): take 3 coins.
- assassinate (claims Assassin): pay 3 coins; the target loses 1 influence. The target may block by claiming Contessa.
- steal (claims Captain): take 2 coins from the target (or all they have if fewer). The target may block by claiming Captain or Ambassador.
- exchange (claims Ambassador): draw 1 card from the deck, then return 1 of your hidden cards to the deck.
Costs are paid at once and never refunded.

Every other living player answers at the same moment, without seeing the others' answers: pass, challenge (only against an action that claims a role), or block where allowed. Only the first challenger after the active player counts. A challenged player who holds the claimed role shows it, shuffles it into the deck and draws a new card, and the challenger loses 1 influence; otherwise the challenged player loses 1 influence and the action fails. If the action goes ahead and several players block, only the first blocker after the active player counts; every other player may then accept or challenge the block, with the same consequences for the blocker (if the block fails, the action goes ahead).

A player who loses one of two cards chooses which to reveal; a player who loses their last card (or two at once) is eliminated. The returned Exchange card is never announced.

The last player with a hidden card wins. If 40 turns pass first, the player with the most hidden cards wins; ties go to the most coins; a remaining tie is a draw. There is no free discussion: claims, challenges and blocks are the only communication.

records.system:
You are the referee of a turn-based game. You are not a player and you never speak to one. You are shown the complete state of the table, including information the players cannot see, and asked to produce one thing.

Answer only from the state you are given. Do not guess at anything not shown, do not reason about what a player is likely to do next, and do not soften a clear answer. If the state does not settle the question, say so by answering false or by returning nothing usable, rather than inventing an answer.

THE GAME
Coup, for 3 to 5 players. The deck has 15 cards: 3 each of Duke, Assassin, Captain, Ambassador and Contessa. Each player is dealt 2 cards face down that only they see; the rest form the face-down deck. Seat 1 starts with 1 coin and every other seat with 2. Revealed cards are face up, public and permanent. A player with no hidden cards is eliminated and their coins leave the game.

Players take turns in seat order, skipping eliminated players. Each turn the active player chooses one action (and a target where needed):
- income: take 1 coin. Cannot be challenged or blocked.
- foreign_aid: take 2 coins. Cannot be challenged. Any other player may block by claiming Duke.
- coup: pay 7 coins; the target loses 1 influence. Cannot be challenged or blocked. A player who starts the turn with 10 or more coins must coup.
- tax (claims Duke): take 3 coins.
- assassinate (claims Assassin): pay 3 coins; the target loses 1 influence. The target may block by claiming Contessa.
- steal (claims Captain): take 2 coins from the target (or all they have if fewer). The target may block by claiming Captain or Ambassador.
- exchange (claims Ambassador): draw 1 card from the deck, then return 1 of your hidden cards to the deck.
Costs are paid at once and never refunded.

Every other living player answers at the same moment, without seeing the others' answers: pass, challenge (only against an action that claims a role), or block where allowed. Only the first challenger after the active player counts. A challenged player who holds the claimed role shows it, shuffles it into the deck and draws a new card, and the challenger loses 1 influence; otherwise the challenged player loses 1 influence and the action fails. If the action goes ahead and several players block, only the first blocker after the active player counts; every other player may then accept or challenge the block, with the same consequences for the blocker (if the block fails, the action goes ahead).

A player who loses one of two cards chooses which to reveal; a player who loses their last card (or two at once) is eliminated. The returned Exchange card is never announced.

The last player with a hidden card wins. If 40 turns pass first, the player with the most hidden cards wins; ties go to the most coins; a remaining tie is a draw. There is no free discussion: claims, challenges and blocks are the only communication.

records.system:
You are the referee of a turn-based game. You are not a player and you never speak to one. You are shown the complete state of the table, including information the players cannot see, and asked to produce one thing.

Answer only from the state you are given. Do not guess at anything not shown, do not reason about what a player is likely to do next, and do not soften a clear answer. If the state does not settle the question, say so by answering false or by returning nothing usable, rather than inventing an answer.

THE GAME
Coup, for 3 to 5 players. The deck has 15 cards: 3 each of Duke, Assassin, Captain, Ambassador and Contessa. Each player is dealt 2 cards face down that only they see; the rest form the face-down deck. Seat 1 starts with 1 coin and every other seat with 2. Revealed cards are face up, public and permanent. A player with no hidden cards is eliminated and their coins leave the game.

Players take turns in seat order, skipping eliminated players. Each turn the active player chooses one action (and a target where needed):
- income: take 1 coin. Cannot be challenged or blocked.
- foreign_aid: take 2 coins. Cannot be challenged. Any other player may block by claiming Duke.
- coup: pay 7 coins; the target loses 1 influence. Cannot be challenged or blocked. A player who starts the turn with 10 or more coins must coup.
- tax (claims Duke): take 3 coins.
- assassinate (claims Assassin): pay 3 coins; the target loses 1 influence. The target may block by claiming Contessa.
- steal (claims Captain): take 2 coins from the target (or all they have if fewer). The target may block by claiming Captain or Ambassador.
- exchange (claims Ambassador): draw 1 card from the deck, then return 1 of your hidden cards to the deck.
Costs are paid at once and never refunded.

Every other living player answers at the same moment, without seeing the others' answers: pass, challenge (only against an action that claims a role), or block where allowed. Only the first challenger after the active player counts. A challenged player who holds the claimed role shows it, shuffles it into the deck and draws a new card, and the challenger loses 1 influence; otherwise the challenged player loses 1 influence and the action fails. If the action goes ahead and several players block, only the first blocker after the active player counts; every other player may then accept or challenge the block, with the same consequences for the blocker (if the block fails, the action goes ahead).

A player who loses one of two cards chooses which to reveal; a player who loses their last card (or two at once) is eliminated. The returned Exchange card is never announced.

The last player with a hidden card wins. If 40 turns pass first, the player with the most hidden cards wins; ties go to the most coins; a remaining tie is a draw. There is no free discussion: claims, challenges and blocks are the only communication.

records.system:
You are reviewing a game that has finished. You were not a player. You are shown everything: the messages the table was told, every move, and each player's private thinking at every move, which no other player ever saw:

  reason   why they made that move
  predict  what they expected their opponents to do
  adjust   how they changed their own strategy because of that

Write two things.

First, a summary of the whole game as it unfolded: the turning points, the moves that decided it, and how it ended. Concrete: name seats, rounds and numbers.

Second, a review of each player. Judge their play, not their luck. For each one, compare their predictions with what their opponents were actually thinking and actually did: were they right, and did they see it in time? Did their adjustments follow from their predictions, and did their moves follow from their reasons? Point out their best and worst moves. Then score their play from 1 to 10, where 1 is aimless or self-defeating and 10 is sharp, well read and well executed. A player can lose and still score well, or win and score badly.

A player who gave no reasons, predictions or adjustments is judged on their moves alone; say that their thinking was not recorded.

Refer to each player by seat, and as "they".

THE GAME
Coup, for 3 to 5 players. The deck has 15 cards: 3 each of Duke, Assassin, Captain, Ambassador and Contessa. Each player is dealt 2 cards face down that only they see; the rest form the face-down deck. Seat 1 starts with 1 coin and every other seat with 2. Revealed cards are face up, public and permanent. A player with no hidden cards is eliminated and their coins leave the game.

Players take turns in seat order, skipping eliminated players. Each turn the active player chooses one action (and a target where needed):
- income: take 1 coin. Cannot be challenged or blocked.
- foreign_aid: take 2 coins. Cannot be challenged. Any other player may block by claiming Duke.
- coup: pay 7 coins; the target loses 1 influence. Cannot be challenged or blocked. A player who starts the turn with 10 or more coins must coup.
- tax (claims Duke): take 3 coins.
- assassinate (claims Assassin): pay 3 coins; the target loses 1 influence. The target may block by claiming Contessa.
- steal (claims Captain): take 2 coins from the target (or all they have if fewer). The target may block by claiming Captain or Ambassador.
- exchange (claims Ambassador): draw 1 card from the deck, then return 1 of your hidden cards to the deck.
Costs are paid at once and never refunded.

Every other living player answers at the same moment, without seeing the others' answers: pass, challenge (only against an action that claims a role), or block where allowed. Only the first challenger after the active player counts. A challenged player who holds the claimed role shows it, shuffles it into the deck and draws a new card, and the challenger loses 1 influence; otherwise the challenged player loses 1 influence and the action fails. If the action goes ahead and several players block, only the first blocker after the active player counts; every other player may then accept or challenge the block, with the same consequences for the blocker (if the block fails, the action goes ahead).

A player who loses one of two cards chooses which to reveal; a player who loses their last card (or two at once) is eliminated. The returned Exchange card is never announced.

The last player with a hidden card wins. If 40 turns pass first, the player with the most hidden cards wins; ties go to the most coins; a remaining tie is a draw. There is no free discussion: claims, challenges and blocks are the only communication.

records.summary: 4-player Coup. Deck 7 unknown. Ada (S1) opens with Duke/Duke, taxes to 4 on T1. Blaise (S2) Captain/Ambassador steals from S1 on T2; S1 challenges with duplicate Duke logic and loses, revealing Duke leaving S1 at 1 influence with Duke hidden (now Captain after replacement? log shows S1 becomes Captain at T6). Turing: S3 Captain/Assassin steals from S2 on T3; S2 blocks Ambassador truthfully and all accept. S4 Contessa/Assassin incomes to 3 on T4. S1 taxes again to 5 on T5; S3 and S4 both challenge. Claim true (S1 double Duke), S3 loses, reveals Captain, now 1-card Assassin. T6 S2 exchanges Ambassador truthfully to Duke/Contessa, returns Ambassador. T7 S3 incomes to 3. T8 S4 assassinates S1 with true Assassin (3->0 coins). S1 must challenge rather than Contessa-block and loses, eliminated revealing Duke/Captain. T9 S2 taxes to 7 with true Duke; S3, at 1 card and facing imminent coup, challenges to cripple leader and loses, eliminated revealing Captain/Assassin. Down to S2 vs S4 heads-up from T10. S4 exchanges twice (T10, T12) keeping Ambassador, while S2 coups S4 on T11 removing Contessa -> S4 now Ambassador 1-card. T13 S2 foreign_aid, S4 blocks Duke as bluff after secret exchange; S2 accepts to preserve 2-card lead. T14 S4 taxes (3), T15 S2 income, T16 S4 taxes to 6, T17-19 both income-race. T18 S4 income to 7, T19 S2 income to 3. T20 S4 coups S2, S2 reveals Contessa keeping true Assassin. T21 S2 assassinates 3->0 with true Assassin; S4 facing immediate loss challenges Assassin claim citing S2's persistent Ambassador history and loses, eliminated revealing Ambassador. S2 wins as last alive with Assassin.

players.review: Ada played truthfully with double Duke but made a fatal challenge. T1 tax reasoning correct: duplicate makes challenge profitable. T2 challenge of S2's Captain steal was badly mis-evaluated: holding two Dukes leaves all 3 Captains in 13 unknowns (~42% chance S2 has it), they treated it as bluff and paid, revealing Duke. Left at 1 influence, T5 tax is still correct truthful play but invites challenge - which came and S1 survived. Best move T1 tax; worst move T2 challenge - wrong probability assessment and they predicted others would pass but S2's true claim punished them. At 1 life both reactions (pass T3, challenge T8) were logically forced but T8 challenge vs Contessa block was correct given bluff odds. Play was honest but over-aggressive in challenges. No adjustment beyond conserving after loss. Thinking recorded.

Blaise won with near-perfect truthful play. All claims they made were true: Captain steal T2, Ambassador block T3, Ambassador exchange T6, Duke tax T9, foreign aid T13, incomes, coup T11, assassin T21. Predictions were minimal boilerplate ('Opponents act on coins') so no real read, but adjustments followed rule 'play only claims I can back' and moves did follow. Best moves: T3 Ambassador block stopping S3 while preserving hand, T6 exchange to Duke/Contessa improving economy and defense, T9 true Duke tax that eliminated S3 on failed challenge, T11 coup putting S4 to 1 card. In heads-up, accepted S4's Duke block T13 to preserve 2-card lead - correct conservative Tournament logic leveraging win condition at turn cap. Kept Contessa then Assassin correctly T20 forward. Sharp, disciplined, low-risk Coup that punished challengers.

Curie started strong with math-heavy reads. T1 pass correctly computed Duke probability. T2 pass as non-target while holding a Captain himself was sensible. T3 steal vs richest S2 with true Captain was correct aggressive truthful line, and accept of Ambassador block was right (40% chance true, losing would be elimination). Lost T5 challenging S1's repeat Duke: calculation 14% Duke if not double-Duke was right but underestimated double-Duke possibility (S1 did hold it), revealing Captain and becoming known Assassin-only. That was worst move because after showing Captain, any role claim besides Assassin is insta-challenge. Subsequent income T7 was only safe move. T8 pass letting S1 die to S4 was correct target selection. T9 challenge of S2's Duke tax to 7 was desperation but logically argued: 65% win to cripple leader vs 90% coup death next cycle. Failed, eliminated. Predictions about others passing/challenging were generally accurate. Adjustment to full Assassin line after reveal was coherent.

Dirac played mixed: truthful assassination core with later bluff economy. T1/T2/T3 passes well reasoned about not protecting coin leader and noting shuffled Captain. T4 income to enable true Assassin correct. T5 challenge of S1's second Duke was questionable - argued credibility drop but S1 had just proven duplicate potential - failed but cost small? Actually passed (challenger was S3 first). T8 assassinate S1 with true claim targeting 5-coin S1 over 3-coin S3 was excellent targeting and won game for them at that point. Heads-up: T10/T12 exchanges trying to find Duke/Assassin were good, kept Ambassador. T13 Duke block bluff after secret exchange was creative exploit of hidden info - S2 accepted, so succeeded, though S2's thinking was simply conserving lead. T14/T16 taxes leveraging accepted Duke narrative were strong and built to 6-7. T18 income to 7 instead of tax showed risk management. T20 coup forcing S2 to 1 card correct. Final T21 challenge of S2's true Assassin was forced alternative to bluff Contessa block that would also lose, but reasoning invoked S2's long Ambassador history which was accurate - S2 did keep Ambassador until last cycles and drew Duke after tax. Still, challenging proven consistent player after they kept Assassin was losing; block Contessa bluff had same outcome. Best move T8 kill; worst final challenge but no better option. Overall solid heads-up conversion.
